opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that embodied intelligence is fundamentally different from language or vision in where its data comes from. For large language models, humanity had already spent decades putting text on the internet. Trillions of tokens were just sitting there, waiting to be scraped and trained on. The same goes for images and videos. But for robots, there is no "internet of actions." Nobody has been recording joint torques, gripper forces, and the precise trajectories of a robot arm folding laundry or assembling parts in a thousand different homes. That data simply doesn't exist yet.

So if you want a robot foundation model that generalizes the way GPT generalizes in language, you have to create the data almost from scratch. And the dominant way people do that today is teleoperation: a human operator controls a robot, usually through a VR headset or a master-slave arm setup, and you record what happens. That works, and it gives you very high-quality data, but it's extremely expensive and slow. One operator, one robot, maybe a few hundred episodes a day if things go well. Hardware breaks, operators get tired, and each scene has to be physically set up. When you compare that to the billions of tokens you'd need to really see scaling laws kick in, the gap is several orders of magnitude.

There's also the diversity problem. It's not just volume. Generalization comes from seeing many objects, many lighting conditions, many layouts, many ways a task can go wrong. In a lab, you tend to collect a lot of data in a few environments, and the model overfits to them. Getting real diversity means going out into the world: different homes, factories, stores. That multiplies the cost again.

That's why in my own work I put a lot of emphasis on synthetic data and simulation. If you can build physically realistic simulated environments, with large asset libraries and procedural scene generation, you can produce enormous amounts of diverse grasping and manipulation data at a tiny fraction of the cost. We've shown, for example in dexterous grasping, that models trained mostly or entirely on synthetic data can transfer zero-shot to real robots with quite strong success rates. Then real-world data plays the role of fine-tuning and alignment, rather than having to carry the entire burden.

Of course simulation has its own challenges: the sim-to-real gap, contact physics, deformable objects, rendering realism. But I believe the path to scale is a pyramid. At the bottom, massive synthetic data for broad generalization. In the middle, human video and other cheaper sources that teach semantics and intent. At the top, a smaller amount of high-quality real robot data. Until the field solves how to fill that pyramid efficiently, data will remain the main bottleneck. Model architectures, compute, and even hardware are progressing quickly, but without data at scale, embodied intelligence can't reach its "GPT moment."

fable-5.1.text:
Because the thing that made large language models work was essentially free. Humanity had already written the internet. Trillions of tokens were sitting there, and all you had to do was crawl them. Embodied intelligence has no equivalent. There is no "internet of robot actions." Nobody spent the last thirty years recording what a hand does when it picks up a cup, with the joint angles and forces and the camera view all aligned.

So you have to produce the data yourself, and every method of producing it is expensive in a different way. Teleoperation gives you the highest-quality demonstrations, but one human operator produces maybe a few hundred trajectories a day. If you want tens of millions, you are talking about building a factory of people. Simulation scales beautifully in terms of compute, but then you pay in the sim-to-real gap, in contact physics, in deformable objects, in lighting. Human video from the internet is abundant, but the embodiment is wrong. A person's hand is not a gripper, and the video does not tell you the forces.

And the deeper problem is that the data is not just expensive, it is also narrow. A language dataset covers almost every topic humans care about. A robot dataset collected in a lab covers that lab, those objects, that lighting, that robot. Change the table height and the policy can fall apart. So you need both scale and diversity at the same time, and diversity is what makes collection truly costly. You cannot just run the same scene ten thousand times.

That is why I say it is the bottleneck rather than model architecture. The architectures, whether diffusion policies or vision-language-action models, are largely borrowed from what already works. What we lack is the equivalent of the pretraining corpus. Whoever solves how to generate diverse, physically grounded, embodiment-matched data cheaply, whether through better simulation, through generative world models, or through some clever way of turning human video into robot supervision, will unlock the field. Until then we are training foundation models on something closer to a few hundred books rather than the whole library.

astra-6.text:
Because embodied intelligence needs data about actions and their consequences, not just what the world looks like. A video might show someone picking up a cup, but it usually doesn’t tell you the forces involved, what the robot sensed, or how it should recover if the cup slips. Those details matter when you actually have to perform the task.

And collecting that experience in the physical world is expensive. You need robots, environments, operators, maintenance, and time. If you want diversity across objects, homes, lighting conditions, and unexpected situations, the collection effort grows very quickly. Repeating a task thousands of times in one lab doesn’t necessarily prepare a robot for someone’s kitchen.

So the bottleneck is not simply getting more hours of data. It’s getting sufficiently diverse, useful interaction data at a cost that lets us scale. Simulation and learning from human videos can help, but we still need to bridge the gap between those sources and what a real robot experiences when it acts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is that embodied intelligence needs data about actions and their consequences. It’s not enough to see an object; a robot needs to learn what happens when it touches, pushes, or grasps it. That depends on the object’s geometry, material, friction, and the surrounding environment.

With language and images, we can draw on enormous amounts of content that people have already created online. For robots, we have to generate much of the interaction data ourselves. That means running hardware, resetting scenes, handling failures, and often having people demonstrate tasks. It’s expensive and difficult to scale.

And volume alone isn’t enough. If we collect a lot of repetitions in one setup, the robot may still fail in a different home or with an unfamiliar object. We need diversity as well as quantity. Simulation can help, but transferring what a robot learns in simulation to the physical world remains a challenge. That’s why I see scalable data collection as such a central bottleneck.
